identification.summary: Storm-2477 is Microsoft's name for the threat actor that develops and maintains the Lumma Stealer (also LummaC2) malware, its command-and-control (C2) infrastructure and the malware-as-a-service (MaaS) offering [S1]. Affiliates pay Storm-2477 for access to a panel where they build malware binaries and manage C2 and stolen data [S1]. This is a financially motivated cybercriminal service, not a state actor, in the sources gathered [S1][S2].
identification.firstObserved: Not stated for the actor in the sources gathered. Microsoft's May 2025 reporting describes activity from at least March 2025 (394,000 infections counted 16 March to 16 May 2025) [S1][S2].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Storm-2477 [S1]. Trend Micro tracks the main Lumma developer as 'Water Kurita' [S3]; the sources gathered do not state that this is the same cluster boundary as Microsoft's Storm-2477, so it is recorded as a vendor alias per the cited report only. Lumma affiliates are separate customers, and ransomware actors Octo Tempest, Storm-1607, Storm-1113 and Storm-1674 are listed by Microsoft as Lumma users; their activity must not be merged with Storm-2477 [S1].

attribution.sponsor: No state sponsor is stated in the sources gathered. Microsoft and partners describe Lumma as a cybercrime tool sold to other criminals [S1][S2].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft attributes development and maintenance of Lumma to Storm-2477 [S1]. No government attribution of Storm-2477 to a named individual or state appears in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Microsoft Threat Intelligence and Digital Crimes Unit (DCU) analysis and a US court order (Northern District of Georgia) enabling domain action [S1][S2]; Trend Micro reporting on the developer's post-takedown statements [S3].

objectives: Financial gain by selling an infostealer subscription service to affiliates; stolen browser credentials, cookies, cryptocurrency wallet data, VPN configurations and documents are then used by customers, including ransomware actors [S1].

sectors: General Windows users, including those searching for software downloads (malvertising) [S1]
Organizations in Canada receiving invoice-themed email [S1]
regions: Global; Microsoft counted over 394,000 infected Windows computers worldwide between 16 March and 16 May 2025 [S1][S2]
targeting.notes: Targeting is opportunistic and driven by Lumma affiliates rather than by Storm-2477 itself [S1].

capabilities.summary: Storm-2477 develops the Lumma infostealer, which steals browser credentials and cookies, cryptocurrency wallet data, VPN configurations and documents; Microsoft identified up to six versions [S1]. C2 servers are hidden behind Cloudflare, with fallback C2 on Steam profiles and Telegram channels [S1]. Affiliates deliver it through malvertising, invoice-themed email, and compromised websites using EtherHiding and ClickFix lures (early April 2025) [S1]. After the May 2025 disruption, Trend Micro reports the operators rebuilt C2 within weeks, shifted to GitHub abuse and fake CAPTCHA sites, reduced reliance on Cloudflare and moved some domains to providers that may be less cooperative with law enforcement [S3]. The developer's claim that a suspected Dell iDRAC flaw was used against its servers is the developer's own statement, not a verified finding [S3].

campaigns.name: Cloudflare interstitial bypass
campaigns.summary: Cloudflare added Turnstile to its interstitial warning page after Lumma bypassed it in February 2025, per a Cloudflare Cloudforce One statement reported by Help Net Security [S4].

campaigns.name: Global Lumma infection wave
campaigns.summary: Microsoft identified over 394,000 Windows computers infected by Lumma worldwide in this window [S1][S2].

campaigns.name: EtherHiding and ClickFix website cluster; Canada email campaign
campaigns.summary: In early April 2025 a cluster of compromised websites used EtherHiding and ClickFix to deliver Lumma, and on 7 April Microsoft observed a Canada-focused invoice-themed email campaign [S1].

campaigns.name: Microsoft DCU and law enforcement disruption
campaigns.summary: Under a court order from the US District Court for the Northern District of Georgia, Microsoft's DCU facilitated takedown, suspension or blocking of approximately 2,300 domains; more than 1,300 were redirected to Microsoft sinkholes. Europol EC3 and Japan's JC3 handled local infrastructure [S2].

campaigns.name: Lumma resurgence
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro reported Lumma returning within weeks, with new C2 infrastructure, GitHub abuse and fake CAPTCHA distribution, less Cloudflare use [S3].

diamond.adversary: Storm-2477, the developer and operator of Lumma MaaS; criminal, no state sponsor stated [S1]. Trend Micro tracks the main developer as Water Kurita [S3].
diamond.capability: Lumma infostealer (up to six versions), affiliate panel for building binaries and managing C2, delivery via malvertising, email, ClickFix and EtherHiding [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: About 2,300 domains disrupted in May 2025; Cloudflare-fronted C2 with Steam profile and Telegram fallbacks; later movement toward other providers and GitHub-hosted delivery [S1][S2][S3].
diamond.victim: Mass, opportunistic victims worldwide; 394,000+ infected Windows computers in two months; Canadian organizations in one observed campaign [S1].
diamond.socioPolitical: Cybercrime economy: affiliates, including ransomware groups, buy access to stolen credentials [S1]. Law enforcement and industry disruption was joint public-private [S2][S4].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints and browsers storing credentials and cookies; cryptocurrency wallets; VPN clients; user trust in CAPTCHA-style prompts and software search results [S1].

gaps: Identity, location and nationality of Storm-2477 operators are not stated in the sources gathered.

Whether Microsoft's Storm-2477 and Trend Micro's Water Kurita are identical in scope is not confirmed; Trend Micro's report was not opened directly (fetch blocked), and the Water Kurita detail relies on search-result summaries of that report [S3].
The Microsoft On the Issues blog, DOJ press release and Trend Micro report could not be fetched; they are cited through search results or secondary coverage [S2][S3][S4].
Current (post-July 2025) activity and any later Microsoft updates to Storm-2477 are not covered by the sources gathered.
Lumma customers (including Octo Tempest, Storm-1607, Storm-1113, Storm-1674) are separate clusters; their intrusions are not Storm-2477 activity [S1].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is the user endpoint and browser credential and session-cookie stores, plus VPN client configurations, which let Lumma customers pivot into enterprise networks [S1]. STEP 2: The service is commodity, resilient and quickly rebuilt after disruption, so defenders should expect continued availability to many affiliates, including ransomware actors [S1][S3]. STEP 3: Template is lure (malvertising, invoice email, ClickFix or fake CAPTCHA on compromised or GitHub-hosted pages), then infostealer, then credential and cookie theft, then sale or reuse by affiliates [S1][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued mass credential theft against Windows users, including DoD-adjacent personnel on personal or unmanaged devices, feeding later account takeover or ransomware. MDCOA is a targeted affiliate using stolen VPN or session material against a defense contractor. Candidate indicators: user-run paste-and-execute (ClickFix) commands, outbound connections to Steam or Telegram profiles used as C2 fallback, new domains behind non-Cloudflare providers, and browser credential store access by unsigned processes [S1][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track Microsoft DCU and DOJ disruption notices and Trend Micro resurgence reporting; a takedown did not end the service [S2][S3]. (2) Authorities: domain seizure and sinkholing were done under US court order by Microsoft and DOJ; military cyber forces would not act on this criminal infrastructure absent separate authority, so coordinate through law enforcement and DC3 channels [S2][S4]. (3) Mission assurance: treat infostealer-harvested credentials and session cookies as a path to mission systems; enforce phishing-resistant MFA and session-token revocation after any infostealer detection [S1]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with the DIB and with Microsoft sinkhole-notification programs where applicable [S2].
